title_en: In the Presence of the Compassionate Lord of Dwarka
translation:
He said, "This is our aarti," and the goldsmith said, "No, this is our aarti." Then, once the matter was clarified, the goldsmith said, "We are of the line of Uda Soni — the Uda Soni who [served] Narsinh — we are Uda Soni, and we recite the aarti of Padmanabh." Then that goldsmith once had a handwritten manuscript come to Narsinh Bhagat. Narsinh Bhagat showed it to me, but I did not ask to keep it, and so that manuscript has since gone missing from their collection. I did not examine the manuscript very closely, and I regret that. But this much is certain: today the heirs of the new generation may not know whether we are, or once were, Uda Soni. Even so, up until about Samvat 2025 a descendant of Uda Soni was still living. It is true that the devotees of Surat district are in no position to investigate such an Uda Soni further. But the goldsmiths who gathered in Valsad had kept alive the memory of Jivandasji's faith — that was the last trace of it.

## In the Presence of the Compassionate Lord of Dwarka

_Dwarka padharya leela joi, manav dehi malvana marag kaha_ (Having gone to Dwarka and beheld His divine play, the path by which an embodied soul may meet the Lord is told.)

In Samvat 1726, on the eleventh day of the bright half of Bhadarva, after coming to Dhanor, Jivandasji Maharaj set out for Dwarka. To attend upon him in service he took his son Shyamdasji along. Having asked leave and taken farewell of the whole Vaishnav community, he set out for Shri Dwarka. On the way a village came — the name of that village is Patdi-Bajanu. The whole company lay down to sleep there; at that time the Vaishnav Jivandasji had gone to sleep, and his son Shyamdasji was pressing his feet, when Maharaj had a dream in which he seemed to be conversing with Kripanath (the Compassionate Lord), and some words were heard being spoken. After he awoke, the Vaishnav Shyamdasji asked Swamiji, "What conversation did you have with the Lord in today's dream?" Maharaj said, "I asked, 'What fruit will You give to the children who come to me in dream [i.e. who turn to me in devotion]?'" Then Vasudevji (the Lord) said: "Whoever wears the tulsi-tilak and walks in it, and keeps to it — for him I shall clear away every fault of karma, and, so that he need not fall again into the wandering of the eighty-four lakh species of birth, I shall grant him, so that he may worship once more, one human birth in which to worship Shri Krishna. The tulsi-tilak is the very sign of Namdev and of Kabirji." Here follows the testimony of Kabirji's own birth-horoscope:

|| Bhekh ||

_Aayo re man sarovar-ko hansa, jinke shrunkhale niranjan vasa ||1||_ (Here has come the swan of Man-Sarovar lake, in whose chain of deeds the Pure One himself dwells.)

_Aayo re malayagiri-ko vasi, kaate karma laage nahi paasi ||2||_ (Here has come one who dwells on the sandal-scented Malaya hill; no bond of karma can ever touch him.)

_Aayo re Sinhal dvipa-ro haathi, aadya purush-ko nirantar saathi ||3||_ (Here has come the elephant of the isle of Sinhal; he is the constant companion of the Primal Being.)

_Aayo re ban kankar-ki jyoti, seep samudra bin jesa moti ||4||_ (Here has come a light out of the forest pebbles — like a pearl formed without sea or shell.)

_Aayo re paras kanchan kaaran, dahekyo kaal dekhyo bhav(jug) taaran ||5||_ (He has come as the cause that turns [base metal] to gold, like the touchstone; having seen and burned away time, [he has come] to carry the age across.)

_Aadya purush-ko sahodar aayo, tulsi tilak naam dhan laayo ||6||_ (He has come as the very brother of the Primal Being; he has brought with him the wealth of tulsi, tilak, and the [Divine] Name.)

_Bast ajuaari so gai re chhapaai, ta kaaran vahalo bhaye sahaai ||7||_ (The bright, shining thing [true devotion] had gone into hiding; for that reason the Beloved became its helper.)

_Udanme aaye das Kabira, bagat kaaran man rakhyo dheera ||8||_ (Into the garden came the servant Kabira; for the sake of the devotees he kept his mind firm and patient.)

_Udyanme dali paayo dhare, marag maanhe julaahe nihaare ||9||_ (In the garden he was found resting on a bough; on the path a weaver caught sight of him.)

_Aap aap maanhi kare vichaara, sundar baalak eh apaara ||10||_ (Within himself the weaver began to wonder — "this is an exceedingly beautiful child.")

_Ke tajiye ke lije uthaai, kartaki gat kali na jaai ||11||_ (Should I leave him, or should I pick him up? The Creator's way can never be fathomed.)

_Ko kahuka larka hoi, hamku aap larega soi ||12||_ (He must be someone's child; that someone will himself come and fight me [for taking him].)

_Jhaar puchhkar jab godo lina, saheb moku beta dina ||13||_ (Setting aside his hesitation, he then took the child into his lap, saying, "The Lord has given me a son.")

|| Sakhi || (a devotional couplet)
_Kabir Kashi khet padhariya, khodya karmana mool.
Chaar charan hoi hari bhajo, bhit gai sanso sool ||1||_ (Kabir went forth to the field of Kashi and dug up the very root of ritual karma. He said: as long as your four limbs stand, sing of the Lord — [do this and] the thorn of doubt melts away.)

Ah! Here has come a pure soul from a spotless place like Man-Sarovar lake, one in whose chain of deeds the Supreme Soul himself dwells. Ah! This is a soul that dwells among the fragrant sandalwood trees of the Malaya region — even crores of karmic bonds cannot touch him. Ah! Here is a soul as exalted as the rutting elephant of the island of Sinhal — the eternal companion and friend of the Primal Being, the Supreme Soul. Ah! He has come to become a giver of light and inspiration to the lowly. He is like a pearl formed without sea or shell — that is, like a soul who has taken incarnation without having to dwell in a mother's and father's womb. He has come, has been revealed, as one identical with — like the very own brother of — the Primal Being, the Supreme Soul. Through this incarnation of his he has brought the wealth of tulsi and tilak, and of the treasure of the Lord's Name. The excellent wealth of devotion to Vishnu had lain hidden; for that reason this Beloved became its helper. The servant Kabirji came into the forest, into the wilderness of ritual karma, and for the sake of the devotees kept his resolve firm with a steady mind. He had taken form on a lotus-leaf in the forest; along that path a weaver noticed him and picked him up. He began thinking to himself — "this is an exceedingly beautiful child; should I leave him lying there, or should I pick him up and take him?" He thought, "This working of God's power cannot be understood. This must be someone's child, and if I take him away, that someone will come and quarrel with me." Wiping away his hesitation, he thought, "God has given this to me" — and understanding it so, took him up into his lap.

That is why the tilak and tulsi belong to Kabirji, taken up chiefly as the sign of the great ones, the supreme devotees. Even so, even if a person does not truly know devotion to Vishnu, yet if he wears the tilak and tulsi and holds to them as a vow, the Lord — pleased by his holding to them with true resolve and steadfastness — will surely spare him the round of the eighty-four lakh species and give him a human birth once more in which to worship. So it was said. (The glory of the tulsi rosary and of the tulsi leaf is spoken of in the Shandilya Samhita, in the Padma Purana, and in the Mahabharata. It is written of in Vasana Samagam, page 130, and in Najar No. 1, page 85: worldly, unenlightened sadhus and mahants who do not honor tulsi — the reason for this is explained in the Kabir-composed Ugra Gita, page 77, where, when Ravana asked his doorkeeper to describe the form of the Siddha [Kabir], the doorkeeper said that the form of Kabira the Siddha is as radiant as the full moon; on his forehead is a white tilak, and around his neck he wears a white tulsi rosary. From this it appears how foolish it is that sadhus who do not honor the tulsi rosary wear instead, around their necks, a black rosary like rat-droppings.)

Vyasji says:

_Vyas tulsi baana hansaka, baba kaam janoU.
Suraapaan aru gang jal, bhela bane na dor ||1||_ (Vyas says: tulsi is the badge of the hansa, the noble devotee — but the sacred thread, mind you, is a [mere caste-]badge. Drinking liquor, and along with it drinking the water of the Ganga — how can these two ever go together?)

Harirama Vyasji says that tulsi is the badge of the hansa — that is, of souls who are devotees of the highest order — while the sacred thread is the badge of the lowly, crow-like people. For drinking liquor, and also drinking the water of the Ganga — how can these two opposite things possibly be done together?

_Vyas baana pahere hansaka, kulka dhaaga khaandh.
So saakut so salil hai, taaku jag le baandh ||2||_ (Vyas says: if one wears the badge of the hansa [tulsi], yet still carries on his shoulder the thread of his own caste-lineage, he is a hypocrite, he is mere outward show — such a one the world's Yama will bind and lead away.)

Harirama Vyasji says that if one who ought to wear the badge of the exalted devotee — the hansa, that is, the tulsi rosary — yet still also wears the sacred thread of his own caste-lineage on his shoulder, then he is a hypocrite; he is superficial, mere outward show. Such a one Yamraj will bind in his noose and carry off to Yamlok.

To one who wears the tilak and tulsi, the Lord grants human birth:

_Hari kiya tab jaaniye, de maanav vataar.
Guru krupa tab jaaniye, bandh chhodaavanhaar._ (Know that the Lord has truly favored you when He grants you human birth. Know that the Guru's grace has truly come upon you when he becomes the one who frees you from bondage.)

We may know that the Lord is pleased with us when He grants us human incarnation, and we may know that the Guru's grace has come upon us when the Guru becomes the one who frees us from the bonds of our worldly existence.

The Padma Purana speaks of the glory of tulsi (as recorded in the Bhaktamal of Amreeka Bhaibhai, page 269):

_Ya drashta nikhiladasangha-shami sprushta-pushpaavani
roganaam abhivandita nirasani sikta-anta-katraasini.
Pratyaasatti vidad-daayini bhagavatah krushnasya samshopita
nyasta tacchcharane vimuktiphalada tasyai tulasyai namah._ (Padma Purana, 79/66)

Here the glory of tulsi is shown in six ways — by her mere sight she quiets all sin; by touch she purifies the body; by mere reverence she cures all diseases; by the sprinkling [of water on her] she keeps even Yamaraj at bay; when properly planted she brings one near to Lord Krishna; and, when offered at His very feet, she grants liberation. To such a tulsi, salutations.

Tulsi Namashtak (the eight names of tulsi):

_Vrunda vrundaavani vishvapujita vishvapaavani
pushpasaara nandini cha tulsi krishnajeevani._ (Vrunda, Vrindavani, worshipped-of-the-world, purifier-of-the-world, essence-of-flowers, Nandini, Tulsi, and life-of-Krishna — these are her eight names.)

Vrunda, Vrindavani, Vishvapujita, Vishvapavani, Pushpasara, Nandini, Tulsi, and Krishnajivani — these are the eight names of tulsi.

_Muleshu sarva-tirthaani, patreshu sarva-devataa.
Shaakhaasu sarva-yajnaadi, tulasi tvaam namaamyaham._ (In her roots dwell all the sacred fords, in her leaves all the gods, and in her branches the sanctity of all sacrifices — to you, O Tulsi, I bow.)

In her root dwell all the holy places of pilgrimage; in her leaves reside all the gods; and in her branches is established the sanctity of all sacrificial rites. To you, O Tulsi, I bow.

Having told Shyamdas this discourse on tilak and tulsi, Jivandasji spoke a sakhi:

_Manav janma moje diya, jaanu hoyego mero das.
Nar apraadhi jeevna, so pade kaalke paas ||1||_ (I gave him human birth, thinking he would become My devotee — but this offending man lived on, and so fell into the grip of time.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says the Lord speaks thus: "In my grace, thinking that this soul would become my devotee, I gave him human birth. But this soul was sinful and wicked, and so again became caught in the bondage of time."

Then, moving on, Jivandasji Vaishnav arrived where the Lord of Dwarka is. Shri Ranchhodrayji's temple faces west, and He is enthroned facing that way. For this reason, how should one circumambulate the original Dwarka, and how should one offer pranam? So he offered pranam with his back turned toward the south. Then, on the second question — the original Dwarka is Pipaji's gate; here at this Dwarka too he offered pranam to all. In this way, offering pranam thus, one's back is not turned toward the Lord's abode in any direction. Jivandasji said that in this world people go about the wrong way, turning their backs toward God. Jivandasji offered his own pranam with his back to the original Dwarka.

[On the occasion of giving a gift, King Nrug suffered; though he met Vasudev, he still went to hell.]

Having told this matter as question and answer, Jivandasji went to make the parikrama (circumambulation). Having made the parikrama: (1) he came down at Swarga-dwar (Heaven's Gate); then (2) he went to Baba Kabirji's platform; (3) from there he went to Mirabai's platform; (4) from there he went to Rohidasji's platform; (5) from there he went to Pipaji's temple; (6) from there he went to Ramanandji's cave; (7) from there he went to Kripanath's in-laws' house; (8) from there he saw Samitri-vaav (this is the name of a stepwell — an image of the Lord had once come out of it); (9) from there he then saw Damodar-koovo (Damodar's well); (10) he had darshan of Nrug-koop (Nrug's well); from there he came to Krukalas Kund. He had Shyamdasji fetch water, and came and stood by the kund. He said to Shyamdasji: "Nrug, a king of the lunar dynasty, son of Ikshvaku, was ruling as a chakravarti [universal sovereign]. He had a vow that he would daily give a thousand cows to Brahmins. Once, one koss [about two miles] from the king's own village, there was another village. There a certain Brahmin was given a thousand cows by the king on the day of Ekadashi. Among them, one cow, unknowingly, got mixed with the king's own herd and strayed back into the king's own cowpen. That cow was due, the next day — Dvadashi — for a ritual act of the Brahmin's fast-breaking. The king said, 'Bring another Brahmin, for the auspicious hour of Dvadashi will pass' — and in the haste, the household's own Brahmin, unknowingly, gave that very cow to a Brahmin named Suman Rishishwar. The Brahmin to whom the cow had been given the day before came looking for her, and it turned out that among the cows given to Suman was his own cow, mixed in. Both men clung to her, each claiming her. King Nrug was sitting down to observe his fast-breaking rite when both of them arrived — for the cow had already been given to the other Brahmin. That Brahmin, taking his gift-cow away, was quarreling with the man trying to take her from him, and the dispute came before the king's court. The first Brahmin said, 'The cow given to me cannot now be given away [to someone else].' The king restored his own cow to him, and said to Suman, 'Do not grieve — for one cow I shall give you a thousand others in exchange.' Suman said, 'Give me back my very own cow; if you do not, I shall burn your body to ashes.' [Under that curse] he [Nrug] lay for a thousand years on the seashore near the Gomti. Then the king said, 'Grant some relief from the curse.' Suman then said, 'By the incarnation of Shri Krishna you will be delivered.' It was by that curse of Suman's that King Nrug fell [into that state, as a chameleon]. When Kripanath Krishna had gone into the forest and grew thirsty, the young Yadav princes went to fetch water. A chameleon would not let go of the well-rope; when Krishna pulled it out, its body turned out to be King Nrug's. Then the messengers of the gods came from heaven's gate and, saying, 'Come to heaven, O king,' took him up to heaven. At that moment he began to praise Kripanath. Shri Krishna said, 'Brother, enjoy the fruit of your own earnings.'"

_Kabir maarun manku, tuk tuk ho jaay.
Vikhki kyari baayke, lunat kyon pachhtaay ||1||_ (Kabir says: I kill my own mind and cut it into pieces. But you, having sown a bed of poison, why do you regret it at harvest-time?)

Das Kabirji says: I kill the desires of my mind and cut them into pieces — in this way I become free of desire. But you, having grown your mental cravings in the poison-bed of worldly lust and desire, why, when the time comes to reap and suffer their evil fruit, do you feel regret?

_Dushtne daan deva thaki, dilnu darad na jaay.
Nrug raja narke gayo, samajethi sukh thaay._ (Giving gifts to the wicked does not take away the pain of the heart. King Nrug went to hell for it — understanding this brings happiness.)

Trikamdas Gordhandas Suryadhodavala writes: giving gifts to bad people does not remove the sorrow within us. King Nrug, by giving such a gift, had to go to hell. So we should understand that such giving ought not to be done, and by understanding this and living accordingly, one attains happiness.

|| Bhekh ||
_Gupat pragat bahu daan, punya je ko karai so paavai, sahit koope parai.
Gaam sangh bhig baaj, gaj kiyo gai paavai.
Aan dharam uvaar, paar pohonche nahi hoi.
Karam kiyo nar dehdhaari, pasuan hoi bhugataan bhao.
Ram bagat bina Farasraam, nar paapi neerfal gao ||1||_ (Whether by secret or by open charity, in whatever way, whoever performs an act of merit shall receive its fruit — yet even so falls into the well. Give away a village, a whole community, horses, or an elephant, and one receives accordingly. Undertake any other dharma however vastly, at any time — even so, none can be delivered by it. If, having taken human birth, one merely performs such deeds, he must still take on animal births to work them off. Parashuram says: without devotion to Ram, a sinner's human birth goes to waste.)

Whether by open or secret charity, in whatever way, whoever performs an act of merit will receive its fitting fruit. Charity of a village, or charity given in full to a whole community, or the gift of horses and elephants — one shall receive accordingly. However broadly one may take up any dharma other than devotion, at any time, still by it none can cross over [attain liberation]. If one abandons the path of devotion to God and lives without it, no good comes to the soul. If, having taken human birth, one merely performs ritual deeds, then even after taking on and enduring four lakh species of animal birth, still he does not cross over. Parashuram says: without devotion to Ram, a sinner's human birth is wasted.

Adhyaruji says:

_Yaag daan ne vrat tape, muj talta nahi avataar._ (Sacrifice, charity, vows, and austerity do not, for me, put an end to incarnation.)

Performing yagna, charity, vows, or austerity does not stop one's taking birth again and again.

Even though the messengers of the gods took King Nrug to heaven, Kripanath Shri Krishna only looked on — so what trust can one place in Vasudev alone? But from before the very mouth of Namdev-Kabirji, one cannot be taken away.

Adhyaruji's word:

_Bhav-narak taale bhakt, parbrahm to avigat.
Jag ghade jeh, nav lahe kon pere teh._ (The devotee is freed from the hell of worldly existence; but the unknowable Parbrahm, the Supreme — He who fashions the world — none can know by what manner He does this.)

The devotee can be rescued from the hell of this ocean of worldly existence by the unknowable Parbrahm, who fashions the world and also unmakes it — none can know how He does this. This same Vasudev fashions crores of universes; yet when a soul is going to hell, Kripanath alone [without the Vaishnav's intercession] cannot save it. A Vaishnav cannot fashion or destroy creation, but he can free a soul that has gone to hell, and he frees it from the sufferings of crores of births. We have seen the example of King Nrug — Kripanath has countless such examples. The sight of a Vaishnav is such that King Janak, by it, emptied the chambers of the twenty-eight hell-pits.

_Laathyo sant tano vaay, chhoota naam tanae mahimaay._ (By the touch of the saint's presence they were freed — by the glory of the Name.)

By the influence of the saint Janak, who traveled in a celestial chariot, the souls of the twenty-eight hell-pits were delivered through the glory of the Lord's Name.

The fruit of the sight of the sage Janak Vipashchit — the fruit of the sight of Vaishnavs — is this: as King Janak, seated in his celestial chariot on his way to his own divine abode, passed overhead, the shadow of that devoted yet detached one fell upon a hell-pit, and all the souls in the twenty-eight crore hells, across the eighty-four lakh species, were delivered. As proof of this, in the account of Janak's life, "the saint's presence" is cited — Adhyaruji says:

_Janak vipashchit keval bhagte-sh narake jeev nihaalya jugate.
Mugat pamaadchaa santo, hari hari || mugat ||21||_ (The wise Janak, by devotion alone, beheld the souls in hell in that manner. The saints obtained liberation — Hari, Hari.)

The learned King Janak, by the mere power of devotion to God — by the power of the Lord's Name — freed, through his shadow, the souls who lay fallen in the hell-pits from the suffering of hell; seeing this, they are said to have been delivered from hell through the power of the Lord's Name.

For this reason it applies to the entire universe. This is the testimony of Parashuram:

|| Kavit ||
_Tirath jovis vaar, vrata chaandraayan kije.
Tulaa tirathme baith, triya de fer na lije.
Gangodar snaan kije, nitya kije pije.
Surabhi savchhi gaay, saral sur devatanku dije.
Ram bhakti vimukh nishkal, saadhan jehi jehi kije.
Nrug narpati jyon Farasraam, daan sahit kooe parai ||1||_ (Make pilgrimage twenty times over, or keep the Chandrayan vow; or, seated at the Tula pilgrimage-place, give even your wife in charity and do not take her back; or bathe daily in the Ganga's waters and drink them; or give a well-formed cow with her calf to the gods — Parashuram says: any practice done in aversion to devotion to Ram is fruitless, whatever it be — like King Nrug, who, together with all his charity, still fell into the well.)

Parashuram says: even if you go on pilgrimage twenty-four times, or keep the Chandrayan vow, or, sitting at a place of pilgrimage, give away a wife in charity by the tula-ritual and do not take her back, or bathe in the Ganga's water and drink it, or give away a cow with her calf like a wish-fulfilling cow, offering her to all the gods — yet if in all this you remain averse to devotion to Ram, then whatever practice or deed you perform is useless. Parashuram says: just as King Nrug, despite performing gifts and alms, was averse to devotion to Ram alongside his charity and so fell into hell, in the same way all actions done without devotion to Ram are useless.

One who is averse to devotion to Vishnu is held in contempt:

_Dhig janma-smin nara-vrudhyaam dhig vratam dhig bahujnataam.
Dhik kulam dhik kriyaa-daakshyam vimukho ye tvadhokshaje._ (Shame on the birth of such a man, shame on his vows, shame on his great learning; shame on his lineage, shame on his skillful deeds — if he remains averse to the Transcendent One.)

If one is averse to devotion to Vishnu, then even holding all three kinds of learning, his birth is to be condemned; his vows too are condemned; his lineage is condemned; and his works of skill and diligence too are condemned.

Pilgrimage-bathing, japa, tapa, and the like are all already contained within the Lord's Name:

_Govindeti sadaa-snaanam, govindeti sadaa japa.
Govindeti sadaa-dhyaanam, sadaa govinda-kirtanam._ (To utter "Govind" is itself constant bathing; to utter "Govind" is itself constant japa; to meditate on "Govind" is itself constant meditation; and constant is the kirtan, the devotional singing, of Govind.)

The Lord's Name, Govind, is itself always equal to bathing. The name Govind is itself equal to constant japa. Govind alone is always fit for meditation. Thus, constant remembrance of Govind is devotion itself.

|| Kavit || (one devoid of the Lord's virtue)
_Tap karm kiye Maandavya, keet saati suri diyo.
Daan nrupati Nrug diyo, baandh ketiya suman kiyo.
Patit raaj dwij Ajaamil, so ekahi naame tar gayo.
Karm dharma bhav bhatak, mite nahin koti karahu jo jagya.
Jyun praachin Barhi kiye, dekhi pashuni (sukh) sankat paryo.
Chaturbhuj Moralidhar, var oojan ananya bin.
Kaho jo kain, insu taryo._ (The sage Mandavya performed austerities, yet was impaled on a stake for once piercing an insect with a thorn. King Nrug gave charity, yet was bound and, by Suman, turned into a lizard. The fallen Brahmin Ajamil, a wicked man, crossed over by the Name alone. Perform crores of sacrifices — the wandering bound by karma and dharma still does not end, just as ancient King Barhi, performing yagnas, saw the suffering of the sacrificed animals and fell into distress. Chaturbhuj says: without matchless devotion to Krishna, the flute-bearer — tell me, who has ever crossed over by anything else?)

Chaturbhuj says: the sage named Mandavya, even though he performed austerities, had in a former birth pricked a butterfly's wing with a thorn, and for that had to be impaled on a stake. King Nrug performed charity, yet the Brahmin named Suman turned him into a hakalas — that is, a chameleon — and cast him into bondage. The king of sinners, the Brahmin Ajamil, was a very great sinner, yet he was saved by the Lord's Name. Even performing crores of sacrifices does not put an end to the wandering bound by the ties of karma and dharma in this ocean of existence — just as the ancient King Barhi, after performing many sacrifices, grew sorrowful upon realizing the calamity that the animals slain in his sacrifices would bring upon him. Chaturbhujdas says: tell me truly — apart from performing sincere, matchless devotion to Krishna, the holder of the flute, who has ever crossed over this world?

As for Chaturbhuj, it is said that the occasion for this saying arose thus: in Vrindavan, he used daily to dance with intense love in Bihariji's temple. One day, while dancing, his loincloth came loose; he was playing cymbals with both hands. If he stopped to tie his loincloth, he would have had to stop playing the cymbals; if he did not tie it, he would become an object of people's ridicule. By the Lord's boundless mercy, two more hands sprouted from his shoulders, and with those he tied his loincloth — thus truly becoming Chaturbhuj, "the four-armed."

|| Sakhi ||
_Kabir duniya dojakh jaat hai, kaaha Hindu Musalmaan.
Ram Rahemaan hi(i) tare khada, chhaand diya ye maan ||1||_ (Kabir says: the people of this world are going to hell, be they Hindu or Muslim. Only Ram or Rahiman stands apart to save — I have given up this pride of opinion.)

Das Kabirji says: the people of this world are going toward hell — Hindu or Muslim, all alike go to hell. For them, whether the name for God is Ram or Rahiman, that God Himself remains apart from all this contention; and as to which of the two names, Ram or Rahiman, is true and which false, I have given up trying to decide that either one is more correct than the other.

_Kabir ham dekhat jag jaat hai, aur jag dekhat ham jaay.
Aisa koi na milai, je pakad chhodaave baanay._ (Kabir says: before our eyes the world passes away, and before the world's eyes we too pass away. I never found anyone who would take hold of my hand and set me free from this.)

The disciple says to the Guru: before our very eyes the world and its people pass away, and before the world's eyes we too go on passing uselessly, wandering about; but we never found anyone who would take our hand and free us from the entanglement of this world.

_Kabir duniyaake main kachhu nahin, mere duniya akath (kaat).
Saahibe door dekhai khada, sab duniya dojakh jaat._ (Kabir says: to this world's people I am nothing, and to me the world is likewise nothing. The Master stands watching from within — seeing that the whole world is going to hell.)

Just as I am worthless to such worldly people, so too is the world of no account to me — because the Master watches, standing from within, seeing that this world is going into hell; but what can I do about it?

Before Lord Krishna's very eyes, King Nrug, having spent a thousand years' lifespan as a chameleon, was afterward taken up to heaven by heaven's messengers. The Lord delivered him, but even He could not prevent his going to heaven [rather than final liberation] — for, as the scripture of the Gita says, after enjoying the fruits of merit in heaven, one must return again to the world of mortals:

_Te tam bhuktvaa svargalokam vishaalam kshine punye martyalokam vishanti.
Evam trayeedharmam anuprapannaa gataagatam kaamakaamaa labhante ||21||_ (Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals. Thus those who follow the ritual Vedic dharma, desiring worldly enjoyments, obtain only going and coming.)

Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit runs out, they attain — that is, must return to — the mortal world. In this way, those who take refuge in the ritual Vedic dharma with desire, longing for worldly objects, attain only going and coming between this world and the next — they go from here to there, and come back again from there to here.

Thus, after enjoying the fruits of merit, one must still, in the mortal world, pass through the eighty-four lakh species of birth. The king suffered great sorrow — this was the power of a Brahmin, over one cow, that sent the king into hell.

_Saakut braahman maskhara, vaaku na dije daan.
Daan sahit narake gaya, padhi padhi chaaro Ved._ (To a deceitful, mocking Brahmin, give no charity. Yet [Nrug,] together with all his charity, went to hell, though [the Brahmin] had studied and recited all four Vedas.)
